title: The Unexpected Benefits of AI on Learning
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles re-reads a study widely reported as proving 'AI use has no beneficial effects on learning' and argues the researchers buried their own positive findings under a framing that only looked at limitations, comparing this to concluding exercise isn't good for you because it increases injury risk. The German economics students in the study used completely unguided, un-primed ChatGPT-style AI (not designed to deepen understanding or check misconceptions) and, while their grades didn't improve because their understanding genuinely wasn't deeper, they did complete tasks faster and passed significantly more exams -- a finding Salles treats as remarkable precisely because the AI received no instructional design at all. His most important interpretive move is separating two claims the original research conflates: AI use didn't produce lower grades or worse reasoning than non-use, it simply let students reach the same baseline performance faster, directly undercutting the common fear that unguided AI use actively damages student thinking. From this, Salles derives a practical two-part classroom implication: first, that 'AI fluency' itself functions as an exam-passing skill worth explicitly teaching, given how many high-stakes papers UK students sit; and second, that if unguided AI already produces this efficiency benefit, deliberately guiding students to use AI as a Socratic tutor -- via a ten-question checklist designed to surface fuzzy understanding, test analogies, and stress-test self-written summaries -- should produce actual grade improvements the original unguided-use study never tested for.
points: Salles's central reframe -- comparing 'AI use has no beneficial effects on learning' to 'exercise isn't good for you because it increases injury risk' -- exposes how a study's own framing choice (examining only limitations) can obscure genuinely positive findings buried in its own data.

The critical distinction the essay pulls out is that unguided AI use didn't improve understanding-driven grades, but it also didn't produce lower grades or worse reasoning than non-use -- it simply let students reach the same baseline performance faster, directly countering the fear that AI use itself degrades student thinking.

The finding is treated as more remarkable specifically because the AI was 'not primed in any way to deepen understanding' -- meaning even the weakest, least pedagogically-designed form of AI use produced measurable efficiency gains, implying deliberately guided use should do considerably better.

The ten-question 'Deepen Understanding Checklist,' designed around treating the AI as a Socratic tutor (surfacing what feels 'fuzzy,' testing where an analogy breaks down, stress-testing a student's own rewritten summary), converts the study's implication into an immediately usable classroom protocol rather than leaving it as an abstract policy conclusion.
quotes: The authors' conclusion is that AI use has no beneficial effects on learning, which has been widely reported. But that is a bit like saying exercise is not good for you because it makes you more likely to get injured.

The German university students, studying economics, did not get higher grades as a result of using AI. This is because they did not deepen understanding. But they did pass more exams. This is even more remarkable when we consider that the AI was not primed in any way to deepen understanding, or to check for misconceptions, or to guide the student.

This is worth repeating, as it dismisses two common fears about the damage caused by AI: AI users did not earn lower grades than non-users, and they did not perform worse in reasoning.
A key takeaway is that students who are AI fluent pass more exams. That's exactly analogous to our schools, where students take around 30 exam papers.
